title: How Poetry Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore how poetry works and how to approach and appreciate it. They open with personal anecdotes about poetry (Josh's rejected poem sent to The New Yorker, Chuck's distaste for it), then cover advice from the essay "How to Read a Poem" on poets.org, including three false assumptions readers make. The hosts trace poetry's history from oral epics like Gilgamesh, Homer, and the Greek and Roman epics, through Chaucer, Shakespeare and Marlowe, the Enlightenment, the Romantics, Whitman, modernism, and the Beat poets. They then explain poetic basics: the three main genres (narrative, dramatic, lyric), reading poems aloud, rhyme including slant rhyme, alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia, meter and feet (iambic pentameter, trochee, dactyl, anapest, amphibrach, spondee-type terms, and the critic/cretic), caesura and enjambment, concrete poetry, and fixed forms (sonnet, ballad, haiku, sestina, villanelle, ode, elegy, epigram, aubade, epistle). They read examples including Dylan Thomas, Philip Larkin, John Ashbery, Robert Creeley, Derek Brown, and David Berman, and discuss metaphor, illustrations (Shel Silverstein), and poetry slams. The episode ends with a listener mail about band names and sign-off.

entities.name: Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night
Farm Implements and Rutabagas in a Landscape

segments.title: Opening banter about poetry
segments.summary: Hosts joke about their feelings toward poetry, Josh's rejected poem sent to The New Yorker, and Chuck's dislike of poetry compared with prose.

segments.title: How to Read a Poem: three false assumptions
segments.summary: Josh summarizes the poets.org essay 'How to Read a Poem' and its three false assumptions: that a poem should be understood on first reading, that it hides a single code, and that it can mean anything the reader wants. They agree poetry should be approached as a carefully crafted work that rewards effort.

segments.title: Poetry's origins and oral tradition
segments.summary: Poetry predates literacy; epics like Gilgamesh were used to memorize stories and history, and poems were meant to be read aloud. Discussion of Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, and Virgil and Hesiod-era Greek and Roman epics.

segments.title: Medieval, Renaissance and Enlightenment poetry
segments.summary: Chaucer wrote in common English rather than Latin, making him hard for modern readers. Renaissance brought Shakespeare and Marlowe and verse drama. The Enlightenment venerated Greek and Roman traditions, and the Romantics rebelled.

segments.title: Transcendentalists, Whitman and modernism
segments.summary: Discussion of Transcendentalists Emerson and Thoreau, Walt Whitman breaking with traditional meter in Leaves of Grass, and the early twentieth-century modernists who favored short, concise poems.

segments.title: Modernists, Beat poets and the poetry-as-life debate
segments.summary: The hosts discuss modernist favorites like E. E. Cummings, Yeats, Gertrude Stein and Sylvia Plath, and the reasons poetry can feel inaccessible when taught backward in time. They then turn to the Beat poets, Ginsberg's Howl and Kerouac.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the discussion of poetry's technical elements.

segments.title: Poetic genres and reading aloud
segments.summary: Narrative, dramatic and lyric poetry are defined, with Shakespeare as an example of dramatic poetry. The hosts note that poems are meant to be read aloud, and that sound effects such as rhyme are central.

segments.title: Sound devices: rhyme, slant rhyme, alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia
segments.summary: Explanation of rhyme, near or slant rhyme (Emily Dickinson's style, bear and far), alliteration, assonance, and onomatopoeia, with playful examples.

segments.title: Meter and poetic feet
segments.summary: Meter as rhythmic structure defined by stressed and unstressed syllables. Iamb, trochee, dactyl, anapest, amphibrach and cretic feet are described, and iambic pentameter is explained with the example of 'partake'.

segments.title: Line breaks, caesura, enjambment and concrete poetry
segments.summary: The hosts discuss line breaks and punctuation, enjambment, caesura, and concrete poetry shaped on the page. Robert Creeley is cited as a master of enjambment.

segments.title: Rhyme scheme and fixed poetic forms
segments.summary: Rhyme scheme notation and fixed forms: sonnet, ballad (alternating tetrameter and trimeter), haiku (five-seven-five), and sestina with repeated end words, illustrated with John Ashbery's poem.

segments.title: Villanelle, ode, elegy, epigram, aubade and epistle
segments.summary: Dylan Thomas's villanelle 'Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night' is read and discussed. Also covered are ode, elegy (Thomas James Martin's poem on five women drowned in a car), epigram, aubade, and epistle (Charles Bernstein's 'Dear Mr. Finelli').

segments.title: Metaphor, illustrated poetry and poetry slams
segments.summary: Metaphor and simile are contrasted using Frost's The Road Not Taken. Shel Silverstein's illustrated poems are mentioned. Derek Brown's poem 'Ringlets' is read, and poetry slams are briefly discussed. Philip Larkin's 'This Be The Verse' and David Berman's poem are read.

segments.title: Listener mail: band names
segments.summary: Listener Matt Burns from Gilroy, California writes about his wife's accidental band name 'Pig Chesterton in the Knuckle Ducks'. The hosts react and mention a band name generator.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and email contact info and sign off.
